title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: This letter had not yet been presented to the Emperor when Barclay, one day at dinner, informed Bolkonsky that the sovereign wished to see him personally, to question him about Turkey, and that Prince Andrew was to present himself at Bennigsen's quarters at six that evening.

News was received at the Emperor's quarters that very day of a fresh movement by Napoleon which might endanger the army — news that later proved to be false. And that morning Colonel Michaud had ridden around the Drissa fortifications with the Emperor and had pointed out to him that this fortified camp, constructed by Pfuel and until then considered a masterpiece of tactical science that would ensure Napoleon's destruction, was in fact an absurdity threatening the destruction of the Russian army.

Prince Andrew arrived at Bennigsen's quarters — a moderate-sized country gentleman's house situated on the very banks of the river. Neither Bennigsen nor the Emperor was there, but Chernyshev, the Emperor's aide-de-camp, received Bolkonsky and told him that the Emperor, accompanied by General Bennigsen and Marquis Paulucci, had gone out a second time that day to inspect the Drissa fortifications, about whose suitability serious doubts were beginning to arise.

Chernyshev was sitting at a window in the first room with a French novel in his hand. This room had probably been a music room; there was still an organ in it on which some rugs were piled, and in one corner stood the folding bed of Bennigsen's adjutant. This adjutant was also there, sitting dozing on the rolled-up bedding, clearly exhausted by work or by socializing. Two doors led from the room: one straight into what had been the drawing room, and another on the right to the study. Through the first door came the sound of voices conversing in German and occasionally in French. In that drawing room, by the Emperor's wish, there was assembled — not a formal military council (the Emperor preferred vagueness) — but a group of people whose opinions he wished to hear given the looming difficulties. It was not a war council but rather an informal advisory session for the Emperor personally. To this semi-council had been invited the Swedish General Armfeldt, Adjutant General Wolzogen, Wintzingerode (whom Napoleon had called a renegade French subject), Michaud, Toll, Count Stein — who was not a military man at all — and Pfuel himself, who, as Prince Andrew had heard, was the driving force behind everything. Prince Andrew had an opportunity to get a good look at Pfuel, who arrived soon after him and passed through to the drawing room, pausing briefly to speak to Chernyshev.

At first sight, Pfuel — in his poorly fitted Russian general's uniform, which looked on him like a costume — seemed familiar to Prince Andrew, though he was seeing him for the first time. There was something of Weyrother, Mack, and Schmidt about him, and many other German theorist-generals Prince Andrew had seen in 1805, but he was more typical than any of them. Prince Andrew had never yet seen a German theorist who combined all those characteristics to such a degree.

Pfuel was short and very thin but broad-boned, of coarse, sturdy build, broad in the hips and with prominent shoulder blades. His face was much wrinkled and his eyes deep-set. His hair had evidently been hastily smoothed down in front at the temples but stuck up behind in comical little tufts. He entered the room, looking around restlessly and irritably, as if afraid of everything in that large space. Awkwardly holding up his sword, he addressed Chernyshev and asked in German where the Emperor was. Clearly he wanted to get through the rooms as quickly as possible, finish with the bows and greetings, and sit down to work in front of a map, where he would feel at home. He nodded hurriedly in reply to Chernyshev and smiled sarcastically on hearing that the sovereign was inspecting the fortifications that he, Pfuel, had designed according to his theory. He muttered something to himself in a bass voice, as self-assured Germans do — it might have been "stupid fellow" or "the whole affair will be ruined" or "something absurd will come of it." Prince Andrew didn't catch what he said and would have passed on, but Chernyshev introduced him to Pfuel, mentioning that Prince Andrew had just returned from Turkey, where the war had ended so successfully. Pfuel barely glanced — not so much at Prince Andrew as past him — and said with a laugh: "That must have been a fine tactical war"; and, laughing contemptuously, went into the room from which the voices were coming.

Pfuel, always inclined to be irritably sarcastic, was particularly upset that day, evidently because they had dared to inspect and criticize his camp in his absence. From this brief encounter with Pfuel, Prince Andrew — thanks to his Austerlitz experiences — was able to form a clear picture of the man. Pfuel was one of those hopelessly and immutably self-confident men, self-confident to the point of martyrdom as only Germans are, because only Germans base their self-confidence on an abstract notion — science, that is, the supposed knowledge of absolute truth. A Frenchman is self-assured because he regards himself personally, both in mind and body, as irresistibly attractive to men and women. An Englishman is self-assured because he is a citizen of the best-organized state in the world, and therefore as an Englishman always knows what to do and knows that whatever he does as an Englishman is undoubtedly correct. An Italian is self-assured because he is excitable and easily forgets himself and other people. A Russian is self-assured precisely because he knows nothing and does not want to know anything, since he doesn't believe that anything can truly be known. The German's self-assurance is the worst of all — stronger and more repulsive than any other — because he imagines that he knows the truth, that is, science, which he himself has invented but which is for him the absolute truth.

Pfuel was clearly of that sort. He had a science — the theory of oblique movements derived from the history of Frederick the Great's wars — and everything he encountered in more recent warfare seemed to him absurd and barbarous: monstrous collisions in which so many blunders were committed by both sides that these wars could not be called wars at all — they didn't conform to the theory and therefore could not serve as material for science.

In 1806 Pfuel had been one of those responsible for the plan of campaign that ended in Jena and Auerstadt, but he saw not the slightest proof of the fallibility of his theory in the disasters of that war. On the contrary, the deviations from his theory were, in his view, the sole cause of the entire catastrophe, and with characteristically gleeful sarcasm he would say: "There, I said the whole affair would go to the devil!" Pfuel was one of those theorists who so love their theory that they lose sight of its object — its practical application. His love of theory made him hate everything practical, and he would not listen to it. He was even pleased by failures, because failures resulting from deviations from theory only proved to him the accuracy of his theory.

He said a few words to Prince Andrew and Chernyshev about the current war, with the air of a man who knows beforehand that everything will go wrong and who is not displeased that it should be so. The unbrushed tufts of hair sticking up behind and the hastily smoothed hair at his temples expressed this most eloquently.
He passed into the next room, and the deep, querulous sounds of his voice were immediately heard from there.
